title: Hadith, Sunnah and Tafsir: How Muslims Interpret
bigQuestion: How do Muslims decide what a verse of the Qur'an means, and why do careful readers sometimes disagree?

story.title: Thirty Volumes for One Book
story.kicker: A student goes looking for one verse and finds a whole wall of books written about it.
paragraphs: Layla's class had been asked to find out what one verse of the Qur'an meant. She had a small copy of the Qur'an at home. It fit in one hand and had a green cover. She thought the job would take ten minutes. Then her teacher sent her to the university library on the South Side of Chicago.

The librarian led her past the fiction and the science books. She stopped at a shelf that ran the length of the wall. "This is one commentary," she said. "Al-Tabari finished it more than a thousand years ago. In this printed edition it runs to about thirty volumes." Layla counted. The books were thick, and every one was about the same small green book in her bag.

She pulled down the volume for her verse. The page did not give one answer. It gave a chain of names, then a report, then another chain, then another report. Al-Tabari had gathered what earlier readers said and then, at the end, told which reading he thought was strongest. Some pages listed six opinions on a single word.

On the next shelf stood a second commentary, by Ibn Kathir, written about 450 years later. Layla opened it to the same verse. It quoted other verses of the Qur'an first, then reports about Muhammad, and then reached a conclusion. The conclusion was close to al-Tabari's but not the same.

Layla wrote in her notebook: "The Qur'an is short. Reading it is long." Muslims have spent fourteen centuries asking what its words mean, and they have written the answers down. This chapter is about those answers, who wrote them, and the tools they used.
story.think: Why might a short book need such a long commentary? What kinds of questions would a reader in the year 900 have asked about a verse?

lessons.title: Reports About the Prophet
lessons.mainIdea: A hadith is a report of what Muhammad said, did or allowed, passed down by a chain of named people.
reading: A *hadith* is a short report. It tells something Muhammad said, something he did, or something he saw and allowed. Muslims believe these reports show how the Qur'an was lived out. A hadith has two parts. The chain of people who passed it on is the *isnad*. The words of the report itself are the *matn*.

A typical hadith begins like this: "A told me, from B, from C, that the Prophet said…" Each name is a link. Muslim scholars checked every link. Did A really meet B? Was C known to be honest? Did C have a good memory? A report with a strong chain was called sound. A report with a weak or broken chain was called weak.

Hadith are not part of the Qur'an. Muslims hold the Qur'an to be the word of God, and hadith to be reports about the Prophet. The two are kept in separate books. But for most Muslims, the hadith are the second source of guidance after the Qur'an, because they show how the Prophet understood it.

words.d: a report of what Muhammad said, did or approved, passed down through a chain of narrators
the chain of names that shows who passed a hadith down, person to person
the text or wording of a hadith, the report itself

look.title: A Hadith on Intentions
look.text: A well-known hadith, reported through a chain that ends with the companion Umar ibn al-Khattab, has Muhammad say that actions are judged by their intentions, and that each person will get what he intended. Bukhari placed it first in his collection.
look.cite: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Revelation, hadith 1 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: What is the matn of this hadith, and what would its isnad be?

check.q: What is the isnad of a hadith?
choices: The chain of people who passed the report down
The name of the book it is printed in
check.why: The isnad is the chain of narrators; the matn is the wording of the report.

check.q: How do Muslims usually describe the relationship of hadith to the Qur'an?
choices: Hadith are chapters of the Qur'an
Hadith are separate reports about the Prophet, the second source after the Qur'an
Hadith are translations of the Qur'an
check.why: Hadith are kept in separate books and are held by most Muslims to be the second source of guidance after the Qur'an.

check.q: Why did scholars ask whether narrator A had really met narrator B?
choices: To see whether the report rhymed
To find the surah it belonged to
To test whether the chain was sound
To count the number of reports
check.why: Checking each link in the isnad was how scholars judged a hadith sound or weak.

lessons.title: Bukhari, Muslim and the Sifting
lessons.mainIdea: In the 800s, collectors such as al-Bukhari and Muslim sifted huge numbers of reports and kept the ones they judged sound.
reading: Two centuries after Muhammad's death, hundreds of thousands of reports were in circulation. Some were sound. Some had been made up to support a ruler, a group or an opinion. Muslim scholars set out to sort them. The most famous were Muhammad al-Bukhari (d. 870) and Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj (d. 875). Each produced a collection called a *Sahih*, meaning "sound."

Al-Bukhari, tradition says, traveled across the Muslim world for years gathering reports. He is said to have examined about 600,000 and kept only a few thousand. Muslim followed a similar method. Four other collections, by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah, joined them. Sunni Muslims call these the Six Books.

Shia Muslims have their own collections, gathered in the 900s and after. The best known is by al-Kulayni (d. 941). Shia scholars also value reports passed through the Imams, whom they hold to be Muhammad's rightful successors. Sunni and Shia collections overlap in many reports but differ in others.

Modern historians read hadith differently. Some accept the traditional sifting. Others argue that even sound chains cannot prove what was said two hundred years earlier. This is an open scholarly debate. Muslims and historians alike agree that the collections shaped Islamic law and life for centuries.

words.d: "sound"; the title of the two most trusted Sunni hadith collections, by al-Bukhari and Muslim
the six hadith collections that Sunni Muslims hold in the highest regard

look.title: The Six Books and Their Collectors
look.cite: Standard dates given in reference works on Islamic studies
look.prompt: About how many years after Muhammad's death (632) were these collections finished? Why might that gap matter to a historian?

check.q: What does the title Sahih mean?
check.why: Sahih means sound; al-Bukhari and Muslim gave that name to their collections of reports they judged reliable.

check.q: Which statement about Shia hadith collections is accurate?
choices: Shia Muslims have their own collections, such as al-Kulayni's
Shia Muslims do not use hadith
Shia collections were written before Muhammad's death
check.why: Shia scholars gathered their own collections in the 900s and after, al-Kulayni's being the best known.

check.q: Why did scholars in the 800s need to sift the reports?
choices: The reports were written in Latin
Some reports had been invented to support a ruler or opinion
The Qur'an told them to burn them
check.why: Many reports were in circulation, and some had been made up; the collectors tried to keep only the sound ones.

lessons.title: The Sunnah as Example
lessons.mainIdea: The Sunnah is the Prophet's way of living, known through the hadith, and Muslims use it to fill in what the Qur'an says briefly.
reading: The Qur'an tells Muslims to pray, but it does not spell out every step of the prayer. It tells them to give zakat, a share of wealth, but does not fix every rate. Muslims believe the Prophet showed how. His way of doing things is called the *Sunnah*. The hadith are the records; the Sunnah is the pattern they show.

The Qur'an itself points to the Prophet as a model. Surah 33, Al-Ahzab, ayah 21, calls the messenger of God a good example. It says this is for those who hope in God and the Last Day. Surah 59:7 says to take what the messenger gives and leave what he forbids. Muslim scholars read these verses as the basis for following the Sunnah.

This is why Muslim practice includes many things the Qur'an does not describe in detail. The number of daily prayers is one. The words of the call to prayer and the details of fasting are others. Different groups of Muslims follow the Sunnah in slightly different ways. They trust different reports, or they read the same reports differently.

words.d: the Prophet's way of living and acting, which Muslims take as a model; known through the hadith
the yearly share of wealth the Qur'an tells Muslims to give to those in need

look.title: A Good Example
look.text: The Qur'an says that in God's messenger there is a good example for anyone who looks toward God and the Last Day and remembers God often.
look.cite: Qur'an 33:21, Surah Al-Ahzab, paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930)
look.prompt: How could one verse like this lead to whole libraries of reports about the Prophet's daily life?

check.q: What is the Sunnah?
choices: The Prophet's way of living, taken as a model
check.why: The Sunnah is the Prophet's pattern of life; the hadith are the reports that record it.

check.q: Which of these is an example of something the Sunnah fills in?
choices: The exact steps of the daily prayer
check.why: The Qur'an commands prayer but does not detail every step; Muslims learn the steps from the Sunnah.

check.q: Why do groups of Muslims follow the Sunnah in slightly different ways?
choices: They trust different reports or read the same reports differently
Only one group has read the hadith
check.why: Differences come from which reports a group accepts and how it reads them, not from different Qur'ans.

lessons.title: What Tafsir Is
lessons.mainIdea: Tafsir is commentary on the Qur'an, and al-Tabari's tenth-century commentary set the model of gathering reports and then judging between them.
reading: *Tafsir* means explanation. A tafsir is a book that goes through the Qur'an, often verse by verse, and explains it. Who is speaking? What does this rare word mean? What event was this verse about? Muslims believe the Prophet was the first explainer. Surah 16, An-Nahl, ayah 44, says the Remembrance was sent down so that he could make clear to people what was revealed to them.

The most famous early tafsir is by Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari (d. 923), a scholar from northern Iran who worked in Baghdad. For each verse he collected reports from the Prophet's companions and the next generations. He gave each report with its chain of names. Then he weighed them. Often he wrote, in effect, "the strongest reading in my view is this one, because…"

Al-Tabari's method became the standard. Later commentators added grammar, law, theology and their own reasoning. A commentator was expected to know Arabic deeply, to know the hadith, and to know what earlier readers had said. The readers of tafsir were students, judges, preachers and anyone who wanted to know what a verse meant.

One point matters for our study. A tafsir is one reader's account of the text. Two commentators can be equally learned and still disagree. When this course says "al-Tabari reads this as…," it is reporting one reading, not settling the question.

words.d: commentary that explains the Qur'an, often verse by verse
Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari (d. 923), historian and author of the most famous early tafsir
the men and women who knew Muhammad in his lifetime; their reports are the first layer of tafsir

look.title: Sent to Make It Clear
look.text: The Qur'an says that God sent down the Remembrance to the Prophet so that he might make clear to people what had been sent down for them, and so that they might reflect.
look.cite: Qur'an 16:44, Surah An-Nahl, paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930)
look.prompt: Muslim scholars read this verse as a warrant for tafsir. What does the verse ask its readers to do?

check.q: What does the word tafsir mean?
check.why: Tafsir means explanation; a tafsir is a commentary on the Qur'an.

check.q: What was al-Tabari's method for each verse?
choices: He wrote his own opinion only
He gathered reports with their chains and then judged which was strongest
He listed the verse without comment
check.why: Al-Tabari collected the reports of earlier readers and then weighed them, often stating which he found strongest.

check.q: Why does the course say "al-Tabari reads this as…" instead of "this verse means…"?
choices: Because the verse has no meaning
Because al-Tabari never wrote about the Qur'an
Because a tafsir is one learned reader's account, and others may differ
check.why: Commentaries are readings by particular scholars; equally learned readers can disagree.

lessons.title: Ibn Kathir and Qur'an by Qur'an
lessons.mainIdea: Ibn Kathir's fourteenth-century tafsir explains a verse first with other verses, then with hadith, and is still widely read today.
reading: Isma'il ibn Kathir (d. 1373) lived in Damascus, in what is now Syria. He was a historian and a scholar of hadith. His tafsir follows a clear order. To explain a verse, he first looks for other verses of the Qur'an that speak of the same thing. Muslims call this method "the Qur'an explains the Qur'an." Then he brings in hadith, then the sayings of the companions.

Ibn Kathir was careful about weak reports. He often warned readers that a story in an older commentary came from Jewish or Christian lore and had no sound chain back to the Prophet. Arabic scholars call such material *isra'iliyyat*. Al-Tabari had included much of it; Ibn Kathir trimmed it. This is one difference between the two.

Ibn Kathir's tafsir is shorter than al-Tabari's, and it has been translated into English and many other languages. In mosques and study groups across the United States it is one of the commentaries most often on the shelf. Other Muslims prefer other commentators. Al-Qurtubi (d. 1273) is valued for law; al-Zamakhshari (d. 1144) for grammar; al-Razi (d. 1210) for philosophy.

words.d: Isma'il ibn Kathir (d. 1373), scholar of Damascus whose tafsir is widely read today
stories from Jewish and Christian lore that entered early commentary; later scholars often set them aside

look.title: Five Classical Commentators
look.cite: Standard dates in reference works on the tafsir tradition
look.prompt: How many centuries separate the first and last of these commentators? What might a later commentator know that an earlier one could not?

check.q: What is Ibn Kathir's first step in explaining a verse?
choices: Looking for other Qur'an verses on the same subject
check.why: His method is often summed up as "the Qur'an explains the Qur'an," followed by hadith and the companions' sayings.

check.q: What is one difference between al-Tabari's and Ibn Kathir's commentaries?
choices: Ibn Kathir trimmed stories from Jewish and Christian lore that al-Tabari had included
Ibn Kathir refused to use hadith
check.why: Ibn Kathir warned readers about isra'iliyyat and set much of it aside; al-Tabari's longer work had included it.

check.q: Which commentator is especially valued for grammar?
check.why: Al-Zamakhshari (d. 1144) is known for close attention to Arabic grammar and style.

lessons.title: Clear Verses and Ambiguous Verses
lessons.mainIdea: Surah 3:7 says some verses are clear and others are ambiguous, and Muslims have long debated how to read the ambiguous ones.
reading: The Qur'an speaks about how it should be read. Surah 3, Al 'Imran, ayah 7, says the Book has two kinds of verses. Some are clear, called *muhkam*, and they are its foundation. Others are *mutashabih*, less certain in meaning. The verse warns against people who chase the ambiguous verses to cause trouble. Then it says that only God knows their true meaning. The well-grounded in knowledge say, "We believe in it."

Here is the puzzle. In the Arabic, the sentence can be stopped in two places. Read one way, it says: only God knows the meaning; and those grounded in knowledge simply believe. Read the other way, it says: only God and those grounded in knowledge know the meaning. The written text has no punctuation to settle it.

Commentators took both sides. Many Sunni readers, including al-Tabari, favored the first reading: some meanings belong to God alone. Some others, and many Shia and Sufi readers, favored the second: deep knowledge can reach the ambiguous verses too. This one pause mark shaped how bold or how cautious a commentator would be.

Which verses count as ambiguous? Scholars list the mysterious letters at the start of some surahs, verses about the end of the world, and verses that describe God with a hand or a throne. How to read those descriptions became a major question in Muslim theology.

words.d: "clear" or "firm"; a verse whose meaning is plain, called the foundation of the Book in 3:7
"ambiguous" or "resembling"; a verse whose meaning is uncertain or has more than one sense

look.title: One Sentence, Two Stops
look.text: Reading A: "None knows its meaning except God. And those grounded in knowledge say: We believe in it." Reading B: "None knows its meaning except God and those grounded in knowledge. They say: We believe in it." The Arabic words are the same in both. Only the place where the reader pauses is different.
look.prompt: Which reading gives scholars more room to explain the hard verses? Why might a cautious commentator prefer the other one?

check.q: What does 3:7 call the clear verses?
check.why: Muhkam verses are the clear ones, which 3:7 calls the foundation of the Book; mutashabih are the ambiguous ones.

check.q: Why can 3:7 be read in two ways?
choices: The place where the reader pauses changes the sense, and the text has no punctuation
The verse exists in two different Qur'ans
Pickthall and Rodwell used different Arabic texts
The verse was lost and rewritten
check.why: The same Arabic words yield two meanings depending on where the sentence is stopped.

check.q: Which group of verses do scholars often list as ambiguous?
choices: Verses that describe God with a hand or a throne
check.why: Descriptions of God in bodily terms, the mysterious letters and end-time verses are the usual examples of mutashabih.

lessons.title: Abrogation: A Debated Tool
lessons.mainIdea: Naskh, the idea that a later verse can replace an earlier ruling, is a tool some scholars use widely and others use hardly at all.
reading: Some verses of the Qur'an seem to give different rules about the same thing. On wine, one verse says there is harm and benefit in it, another tells believers not to pray while drunk, and another calls it something to avoid. Muslim scholars explained this as *naskh*, abrogation. Rules came in stages; the later verse replaced the earlier.

The idea rests partly on Surah 2, Al-Baqarah, ayah 106, which says that when God causes a verse to be forgotten or sets it aside, He brings one better or like it. Classical scholars wrote whole books listing which verses abrogated which. Their lists did not agree. Some counted more than two hundred cases; al-Suyuti (d. 1505) trimmed the list to about twenty.

The debate matters most for the verses on fighting. Some medieval jurists argued that Surah 9:5, the so-called sword verse, canceled the many verses that urge peace and patience. Most classical and modern scholars disagree. They read 9:5 as tied to a specific broken treaty, and they hold that verses such as 2:256, "there is no compulsion in religion," still stand.

Modern Muslim scholars take a range of views. Some keep the classical tool. Some, like the Egyptian scholar Muhammad Abduh (d. 1905), reduced its use sharply. Some argue that 2:106 refers to earlier scriptures, not to verses within the Qur'an. This is an ongoing discussion inside the tradition, and this course reports it without deciding it.

words.d: abrogation; the idea that a later verse or ruling replaces an earlier one
Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti (d. 1505), Egyptian scholar who reduced the list of abrogated verses to about twenty

look.title: Something Better or Like It
look.text: The Qur'an says that whatever verse God sets aside or causes to be forgotten, He brings a better one or one like it, and asks whether the hearer does not know that God is able to do all things.
look.cite: Qur'an 2:106, Surah Al-Baqarah, paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930)
look.prompt: Some scholars read "verse" here as a verse of the Qur'an; others read it as an earlier scripture. How would each reading change the use of naskh?

check.q: What does naskh mean?
choices: Abrogation, a later ruling replacing an earlier one
check.why: Naskh is the idea that a later verse or ruling sets aside an earlier one; scholars debate how often it applies.

check.q: How did al-Suyuti differ from earlier scholars on abrogation?
choices: He listed more than five hundred cases
He reduced the list to about twenty cases
check.why: Al-Suyuti trimmed the long classical lists to roughly twenty verses.

check.q: How do most classical and modern scholars read 9:5 in relation to 2:256?
choices: 9:5 concerns a specific broken treaty, and 2:256 still stands
check.why: Mainstream scholars tie 9:5 to its occasion and hold that "no compulsion in religion" remains in force; a minority of medieval jurists argued otherwise.

lessons.title: Sunni and Shia Readings
lessons.mainIdea: Sunni and Shia Muslims read the same Qur'an but differ on who may interpret it and on the meaning of certain verses.
reading: Sunni and Shia Muslims share one Qur'an, with the same 114 surahs in the same order. The split between them began over leadership after Muhammad's death in 632. Sunnis accepted Abu Bakr as the first caliph, the community's leader. Shia Muslims held that Ali, the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law, should have led, and that leadership passed through his family, the Imams.

This shapes interpretation. For Shia Muslims, the Imams are guided interpreters of the Qur'an, and their sayings carry great weight in tafsir. Shia commentators such as al-Tabrisi (d. 1153) read verses about "those in authority" (4:59) and "the people of the house" (33:33) as referring to the Prophet's family. Sunni commentators read those verses more broadly.

A small example shows the pattern. Surah 5:6 describes washing before prayer and mentions the feet. Because of how the Arabic word for feet is voweled, the verse can be read as "wash your feet" or "wipe your feet." Most Sunni scholars read "wash," supported by hadith. Most Shia scholars read "wipe," supported by their reports. The text is shared; the reading differs.

Sunnis make up the large majority of Muslims worldwide, commonly estimated at 85 to 90 percent. Shia Muslims live mainly in Iran, Iraq, Bahrain, Azerbaijan and Lebanon, with communities everywhere, including Chicago. Both groups pray, fast, give zakat and make the pilgrimage, and both hold the Qur'an as God's word.

words.d: the leader of the Muslim community after Muhammad, as Sunni Muslims understand the office
for Shia Muslims, one of the guided leaders from the Prophet's family; also, more generally, a prayer leader
a Shia commentator (d. 1153) whose tafsir is widely used among Shia Muslims

look.title: Wash or Wipe
look.text: Surah 5:6 tells believers preparing for prayer to wash their faces and hands, wipe their heads, and then mentions their feet. In the Arabic, a single vowel mark decides whether "feet" goes with "wash" or with "wipe." Sunni scholars, citing hadith, generally read "wash." Shia scholars, citing their own reports, generally read "wipe."
look.prompt: What two kinds of evidence are the scholars using here, and why does each side's evidence point a different way?

check.q: What do Sunni and Shia Muslims share?
choices: The same Qur'an with the same 114 surahs
check.why: Both read the same Qur'an; they differ over leadership, interpretation and some readings.

check.q: For Shia Muslims, who are the guided interpreters of the Qur'an?
choices: The Imams from the Prophet's family
check.why: Shia Muslims hold that the Imams, descended from Ali and Fatima, interpret the Qur'an with divine guidance.

check.q: Why do Sunni and Shia scholars read the word "feet" in 5:6 differently?
choices: The Shia text leaves out the word
The Sunni text adds an extra verse
A vowel mark in the Arabic can be read two ways, and each side follows its own reports
check.why: The consonants are the same; the vowel and the supporting hadith decide whether feet are washed or wiped.

lessons.title: Sufi Readings: The Inner Sense
lessons.mainIdea: Sufi readers look for an inner meaning beneath a verse's plain sense, and many hold that the two levels go together.
reading: *Sufism* is the name for the mystical side of Islam. It is the search for closeness to God through prayer, remembrance and self-discipline. Sufis are found among both Sunni and Shia Muslims. When Sufis read the Qur'an, they often look for an inner meaning, called *batin*. It lies beneath the outer or plain meaning, called *zahir*.

Take Surah 24, An-Nur, ayah 35, the Light Verse. It says God is the light of the heavens and the earth, and compares that light to a lamp in a niche, in a glass shining like a star, lit from a blessed olive tree. The scholar al-Ghazali (d. 1111) wrote a whole short book on this one verse. He read the lamp, the glass and the niche as levels of the human soul and mind.

Sufi commentators such as al-Qushayri (d. 1072) went verse by verse looking for such senses. Most of them insisted that the inner meaning never cancels the outer one. A verse about Musa (Moses) and Pharaoh is still about Musa and Pharaoh. It may also be about the struggle inside each person. Critics within Islam warned that inner readings could drift too far from the text. Sufis answered that the Qur'an itself invites reflection.

words.d: the mystical tradition within Islam, focused on closeness to God through remembrance and discipline
the outer or plain meaning of a verse
the inner or hidden meaning of a verse, which Sufi readers seek beneath the plain sense

look.title: The Light Verse
look.text: The Qur'an says God is the light of the heavens and the earth, and likens that light to a niche holding a lamp; the lamp is in a glass, the glass like a shining star, lit from a blessed olive tree that is neither of the east nor of the west, whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it. Light upon light, it says; God guides to His light whom He wills.
look.cite: Qur'an 24:35, Surah An-Nur, paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930)
look.prompt: Al-Ghazali read the niche, glass and lamp as parts of the human mind. What is the plain sense, and what does the inner reading add?

check.q: What do Sufi readers mean by batin?
choices: The inner meaning beneath the plain sense
check.why: Batin is the inner sense; zahir is the outer or plain sense.

check.q: Which verse did al-Ghazali write a short book about?
check.why: Al-Ghazali's Niche of Lights is a reflection on 24:35.

check.q: What did most Sufi commentators say about the outer meaning?
choices: It still stands; the inner meaning adds to it
It is found only in hadith
check.why: Sufi readers such as al-Qushayri held that the inner sense never cancels the plain sense.

lessons.title: The Ulama and the Schools of Law
lessons.mainIdea: The ulama are Islam's trained scholars, and their schools of law turned the Qur'an and Sunnah into rules for daily life in more than one way.
reading: The *ulama* are the learned: people trained in Arabic, the Qur'an, hadith and law. There is no single head of Islam, no one person who decides what the Qur'an means. Instead, the ulama debate, teach and issue opinions. A trained scholar's opinion on a question is a *fatwa*. Another scholar may disagree, and often does.

Between the 700s and 900s, the ulama formed schools of law, called *madhhabs*. Sunni Muslims have four main schools, named for their founders: Hanafi (Abu Hanifa, d. 767), Maliki (Malik ibn Anas, d. 795), Shafi'i (al-Shafi'i, d. 820) and Hanbali (Ahmad ibn Hanbal, d. 855). Most Shia Muslims follow the Ja'fari school, named for the Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (d. 765).

The schools agree on most things and differ on details: how to hold the hands in prayer, what breaks a fast, how contracts work. They differ because they weigh the sources differently. One school leans harder on hadith; another gives more room to reasoning by analogy or to local custom. A Muslim in Chicago may follow any school. A mosque in Bridgeview and a mosque on Devon Avenue may follow different ones and pray side by side.

The scholars also distinguish levels of authority. The Qur'an comes first. The Sunnah comes second. Then come the agreement of scholars and reasoning from the first two. Later law books are human work and can be revised. This ranking is itself part of how Muslims read the Qur'an: it tells them which text settles a question.

words.d: the trained religious scholars of Islam; there is no single head, so they teach and debate
a school of Islamic law; Sunni Muslims have four main ones, most Shia Muslims follow the Ja'fari school
a trained scholar's opinion on a question of Islamic law; not binding on other scholars

look.title: Founders of the Schools of Law
look.unit: year of death CE, commonly given
look.cite: Standard dates in reference works on Islamic law
look.prompt: All five founders died within one century. What was happening in the Muslim world that made this the century for building law?

check.q: Who are the ulama?
choices: Islam's trained scholars of Qur'an, hadith and law
check.why: The ulama are the learned; because Islam has no single head, they teach, debate and give opinions.

check.q: How many main schools of law do Sunni Muslims have?
check.why: The four Sunni schools are Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali.

check.q: Why do the schools differ on details?
choices: They weigh the sources differently, such as hadith versus analogy
Only one school has read the hadith
The Qur'an assigns each school a region
check.why: The schools share the same sources but rank and use them differently, so their rulings differ on details.

lessons.title: One Verse, Two Commentaries
lessons.mainIdea: Reading a verse with two commentaries side by side shows that interpretation is a conversation across centuries, not a single verdict.
reading: Surah 2, Al-Baqarah, ayah 238, tells believers to guard the prayers and "the middle prayer." Which prayer is the middle one? The verse does not say. Muslims pray five times a day, so the question is real, and readers have argued it since the first century of Islam.

Al-Tabari gathers the reports. Some companions said it was the afternoon prayer, 'asr. Others said the dawn prayer, or the noon prayer, or the sunset prayer. He lists each opinion with its chain of names. Then he judges. He favors 'asr, because a hadith reports the Prophet naming it during a battle. Ibn Kathir, four centuries later, reaches the same conclusion by a shorter road: he cites the hadith directly, then notes the other views briefly.

Read the two together and you can see the tradition at work. Both scholars use the same tools: the text, the reports, the companions' views. Al-Tabari shows all his work; Ibn Kathir shows the strongest evidence. Neither says the other views are foolish. A student who reads only one commentary sees a verdict. A student who reads two sees a conversation.

This is the skill this chapter has been building. When you meet a claim about what the Qur'an means, ask: which reader, which tools, which century? The answer will not tell you whether the claim is true. It will tell you where it comes from, and that is what the study of a scripture can offer.
